text.en: Why does the coil of an electric heater glow red hot while the copper wire that brings current to it stays cool? Both carry the same current, so the answer must lie in a property of the material, called resistance.

Georg Simon Ohm, a German physicist, found the relation between the potential difference across a conductor and the current through it.
Ohm's law states that at constant temperature, the steady current I through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference V across its ends.
So V divided by I is a constant for a given conductor, and we write V = I R.
The constant R is the resistance, the property of a material to oppose the flow of charges and hence the passage of current.
Resistance is defined as the ratio of the potential difference across the ends of a conductor to the current through it, R = V / I.
Its SI unit is the ohm, symbol Omega; a conductor has a resistance of one ohm if one ampere flows through it when one volt is maintained across its ends.
Because V is proportional to I, the graph of V against I for a conductor is a straight line, and its slope gives the resistance.
If you replace a nichrome wire with copper or aluminium in the same circuit, the current changes for the same potential difference, which shows that resistance differs from material to material.
Resistance depends on the material, the temperature, the length and the area of cross section of the conductor.
The reciprocal of resistance is conductance G = 1/R, which measures how easily a material lets charges pass, and its unit is ohm to the power minus one, also called mho.
Ohm's law holds only when the temperature stays constant; a heating wire does not give a straight V-I line at all temperatures.
In every problem you can find any one of V, I or R when the other two are known, by using V = I R in the right form.

problem.en: Calculate the resistance of a conductor through which a current of 2 A passes when the potential difference between its ends is 30 V.

text.en: Given I = 2 A and V = 30 V.
From Ohm's law R = V / I.

why.en: Divide and give the unit ohm.

text.en: Check: I R = 2 x 15 = 30 V, which matches.

prompt.en: State Ohm's law, define resistance and describe the V-I graph.

requiredIdeas.en: Current proportional to potential difference at constant temperature

commonMisconceptions.en: Saying resistance depends on the current

points.en: Ohm's law: at constant temperature V is proportional to I, so V = I R.
R = V / I and its SI unit is the ohm; 1 ohm = 1 V per A.
The V-I graph of an ohmic conductor is a straight line.
